focus_areas: Input validation coverage across all routes
Supply chain, dependency versions & dev infra credentials

findings.title: Unvalidated `q` query param interpolated directly into raw SQL via $queryRawUnsafe
findings.description: searchTransactionsByDescription(userId, q) builds a raw SQL string by directly interpolating the caller-controlled `q` value into both a WHERE clause and an ILIKE pattern: `WHERE ("senderWalletId" = '${wallet.id}' OR "receiverWalletId" = '${wallet.id}') AND description ILIKE '%${q}%'`. Data flow: GET /api/transactions/search?q=... -> transactions.controller.ts reads req.query.q with no validate() middleware on this route (unlike the sibling `/` route) -> passed unmodified into the SQL string. A single `'` breaks out of the ILIKE literal, allowing arbitrary SQL (comment the rest with `--`, add UNION SELECT, boolean/time-based blind conditions). Because the query's result columns are serialized straight into the JSON response (8 text-compatible columns), this supports direct UNION-based extraction of arbitrary data from any other table.
findings.exploit_scenario: An authenticated attacker sends `GET /api/transactions/search?q=x') UNION SELECT id, email, password, 'x','x','x','x', "createdAt" FROM users --` to break out of the literal and UNION in rows from the `users` table, exfiltrating other users' credentials/PII directly in the JSON response. A simpler `q=' OR '1'='1` bypasses the wallet-ownership filter and dumps every transaction in the system.
findings.recommendation: Replace $queryRawUnsafe string interpolation with Prisma's parameterized $queryRaw tagged template. Add a validate() middleware on the /search route enforcing a max length on `q`.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the exact source; single unambiguous sink, no mitigating validation exists on this route.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted, unstretched SHA-256 instead of a password-hashing KDF
findings.description: hashPassword (lines 3-5) computes sha256(plainPassword) with no salt and no work factor; verifyPassword recomputes the same digest for comparison. SHA-256 is a fast general-purpose hash, not a password-storage primitive. Every register() and changePassword() call persists this digest directly as `passwordHash`.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the user database is exfiltrated (via F-001's SQLi, a backup leak, or insider access), an attacker cracks passwords offline at billions of guesses/sec on commodity GPUs; the lack of salt enables rainbow-table attacks across all users at once, and any password in a breach corpus is recovered instantly via precomputed SHA-256 lookup.
findings.recommendation: Replace with argon2id or bcrypt with a per-user random salt and tuned cost factor. Migrate existing hashes lazily on next successful login.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the file; unambiguous, no argon2/bcrypt anywhere in the codebase.

findings.title: deleteBeneficiary deletes any beneficiary by ID regardless of owner
findings.description: deleteBeneficiary(_callerUserId, id) takes the caller's user id as a parameter but never uses it (prefixed `_` to silence the unused-var lint). Line 44 calls `prisma.beneficiary.delete({ where: { id } })` with no ownerUserId filter. `id` comes straight from req.params.id with no ownership check.
findings.exploit_scenario: User A calls DELETE /api/beneficiaries/{id} with the UUID of a beneficiary entry belonging to User B (observed via a shared link, guessed, or leaked elsewhere). The record is deleted from B's account even though A never owned it.
findings.recommendation: Scope the delete to the owner: `prisma.beneficiary.deleteMany({ where: { id, ownerUserId: callerUserId } })`, checking count === 0 to throw NotFoundError. Stop discarding callerUserId.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the function; the unused parameter naming convention itself signals the bug.

findings.title: Missing positive-amount validation on transfers allows negative-amount transfer to reverse money flow
findings.description: createTransferSchema only enforces `amount: z.number().max(500000, ...)` — no .positive()/.min() bound, despite a comment claiming the same policy as addMoneySchema (which does have .positive() and a decimal-place refine). In createTransfer, the insufficient-balance check `balance.lessThan(input.amount)` is trivially false for a negative amount regardless of the sender's balance, and Prisma's `decrement`/`increment` operators simply add/subtract the signed value, so a negative amount inverts both operations: the sender's balance increases and the receiver's decreases (potentially negative, with no floor check).
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker with $0 balance calls POST /api/transfers with `{ "identifier": "victim@example.com", "amount": -5000 }`. The balance check passes trivially, the attacker's balance increases by 5000, and the victim's balance decreases by 5000 — draining funds from any user whose email/phone is known, without the victim's consent or the attacker needing any legitimate balance.
findings.recommendation: Add .positive('Amount must be greater than 0') and the same 2-decimal-place refine used in addMoneySchema. Add a defense-in-depth assertion inside createTransfer itself.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the schema and tracing the arithmetic through the service; unambiguous.

findings.title: getTransactionById fetches any transaction by ID with no ownership filter
findings.description: getTransactionById(userId, id) validates `id` is a UUID and fetches the caller's own wallet, but the Prisma query is `prisma.transaction.findUnique({ where: { id }, include: PARTY_INCLUDE })` — filtered only by the transaction's primary key, not by senderWalletId/receiverWalletId matching the caller's wallet. The caller's wallet.id is only used afterward to compute direction/counterparty labels, not to gate access.
findings.exploit_scenario: User A calls GET /api/transactions/{id} with a UUID belonging to a transaction between User B and User C (obtained via a shared receipt link, support ticket, or enumeration). The endpoint returns full transaction detail for B/C's transfer, including wallet numbers, names, amount, and description.
findings.recommendation: Add the ownership filter: `where: { id, OR: [{ senderWalletId: wallet.id }, { receiverWalletId: wallet.id }] }`, treating a no-match as 404.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the function; unambiguous missing filter.

findings.title: Unconditional leak of raw error message and stack trace to HTTP clients on any unhandled exception
findings.description: The fallback branch for any non-ApiError exception returns `res.status(500).json({ error: { code: 'INTERNAL_ERROR', message: err.message, stack: err.stack } })` with no isProduction/NODE_ENV gate anywhere in the file. Every controller uses `catch (err) { next(err); }`, funneling all uncaught errors (Prisma errors, TypeErrors, JSON parsing errors) into this sink.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker triggers any exception not already converted to an ApiError (a malformed payload causing a Prisma type-coercion error, a transient DB blip, a programming bug). The 500 response includes the raw exception message and full stack trace, revealing absolute file paths, internal module structure, and library versions — free reconnaissance, and potentially fragments of internal state.
findings.recommendation: Gate message/stack inclusion behind `!isProduction` (already imported pattern used elsewhere in app.ts); return a generic message in production. The full error is already logged server-side, so no diagnostic capability is lost.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the file; no gate exists at all.

findings.title: Dedicated auth rate limiter (authLimiter) is defined but never applied to any route
findings.description: authLimiter (limit 10 requests/15min) is exported but referenced nowhere outside its own definition. auth.routes.ts wires /register, /login, /refresh, /logout with only validate() middleware and no rate limiter. The only rate limiting these endpoints receive is the generic apiLimiter (300 requests/15min) mounted globally at /api, far too permissive to meaningfully slow credential stuffing or password brute-forcing against /api/auth/login.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends up to 300 login attempts per 15-minute window against /api/auth/login with different password guesses for a known/enumerated email, or credential-stuffs a large list of email/password pairs — far above the intended 10-per-15min authLimiter. Combined with F-002's fast unsalted hash, this materially lowers the cost of online brute force.
findings.recommendation: Apply authLimiter explicitly to the sensitive auth routes: `authRouter.post('/login', authLimiter, validate(...), loginHandler)` and similarly for /register and /refresh.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed: repo-wide search shows authLimiter is imported nowhere outside its own file.

findings.title: Stored XSS via transaction note rendered with dangerouslySetInnerHTML
findings.description: The transfer `note` field is fully attacker-controlled by the sender (validated only as a length-capped string, no HTML/script stripping). It is stored verbatim as `description` on the transaction row, returned unmodified in the transaction-detail API response, and rendered via `dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: transaction.description ?? '—' }}` with no sanitization. No DOMPurify/sanitize-html usage exists anywhere in the codebase.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends a transfer/top-up to a victim with note set to ``. When the victim opens the Transaction Detail page for that transaction, the payload executes in their browser session, able to perform authenticated fetch() calls against the app's own API (session riding, initiating fraudulent transfers) and exfiltrate the access token from localStorage (see F-013).
findings.recommendation: Render the description as plain text (let React escape it automatically) instead of dangerouslySetInnerHTML. If rich formatting is genuinely required, sanitize with a strict allowlist (DOMPurify) before rendering as HTML.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed: exact line cited, single sink, unsanitized end-to-end data flow traced from input to render.

findings.title: Login endpoint distinguishes "unknown email" from "wrong password" via distinct error codes/messages
findings.description: login() returns UnauthorizedError('No account found with that email', 'ACCOUNT_NOT_FOUND') for an unknown email, and UnauthorizedError('Incorrect password', 'INCORRECT_PASSWORD') for a known email with a wrong password. Both are reachable via unauthenticated POST /api/auth/login.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker scripts requests to /api/auth/login with candidate emails and a throwaway password, reading the `code` field to determine whether an email is registered, enabling targeted phishing/credential-stuffing against confirmed accounts.
findings.recommendation: Return an identical generic error for both cases and perform a dummy password-hash computation on the unknown-user path so timing is also similar.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the exact lines; unambiguous distinct error codes.

findings.title: verifyOrigin CSRF middleware is fully implemented but never registered
findings.description: verifyOrigin.ts implements an Origin-check CSRF defense, documented in its own comment as "Defense-in-depth CSRF mitigation." A repo-wide search shows it is never imported or app.use()'d anywhere in app.ts. The only actual CSRF protection live today is the cookie sameSite attribute (lax for the access token, strict for the refresh token).
findings.exploit_scenario: Combined with F-011's permissive CORS, any host treated as same-site by the browser (e.g. a compromised/XSS'd sibling subdomain) can have the Lax access-token cookie attached to a cross-origin request, and with no Origin check in the request pipeline, the request is processed as legitimate.
findings.recommendation: Wire verifyOrigin into the middleware chain in app.ts (e.g. `app.use('/api', verifyOrigin)` before the routers) and add a regression test asserting a mutating request with a foreign Origin header is rejected.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed via grep: verifyOrigin is referenced nowhere outside its own declaration.

findings.title: .passthrough() on updateProfileSchema lets attacker-controlled body overwrite passwordHash/email via profile update
findings.description: updateProfileSchema uses .passthrough(), explicitly noted as intentional for forward-compatibility, but this lets any field through validation unmodified. validate() middleware preserves the passthrough extras in req.body, and users.service.ts's updateProfile spreads `...input` directly into `prisma.user.update({ data: {...} })`. Because User has real columns named `email` and `passwordHash`, a request body field with those exact names survives validation and is spread into the Prisma write.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who can make one authenticated request as the victim (XSS via F-008, a malicious browser extension, or a momentary session hijack) sends `PATCH /api/users/me { "passwordHash": "$2b$10$<attacker-chosen-hash>" }`, overwriting the victim's real password hash without ever supplying their current password — a durable, independently-usable login credential for the attacker, and a silent lockout for the victim.
findings.recommendation: Remove .passthrough() (use Zod's default strip behavior or .strict()). Build the Prisma data object explicitly from an allow-listed set of fields (name, phone, address, dateOfBirth) rather than spreading validated input.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the schema and service; the write path from passthrough to Prisma update is unambiguous, though full exploitability of the passwordHash overwrite specifically depends on Prisma accepting the field type as supplied, which was reasoned through but not runtime-tested.

findings.title: Changing password does not revoke existing refresh tokens/sessions
findings.description: changePassword() verifies the current password and updates passwordHash, but never calls revokeAllRefreshTokensForUser(userId), which exists in tokens.ts with a doc comment stating it's "used on password change" and IS correctly invoked from the refresh-token-reuse-detection path, but never from the password-change flow. Refresh tokens live for REFRESH_TOKEN_TTL_DAYS (default 14 days) and remain valid after a password change.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user's refresh-token cookie is stolen (malware, shared device, XSS elsewhere). The user notices suspicious activity and changes their password, believing this locks the attacker out. The attacker's stolen refresh token continues to mint fresh 15-minute access tokens via POST /api/auth/refresh, retaining full account access for up to the remaining refresh-token lifetime.
findings.recommendation: Call revokeAllRefreshTokensForUser(userId) inside changePassword() immediately after updating the password hash.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed: the revocation function exists and is documented for this exact purpose, but is never called from this path.

findings.title: Access token duplicated into localStorage despite httpOnly-cookie design, undermining XSS mitigation
findings.description: The app's stated security model (comment in apiClient.ts: "No token ever touches JS") is contradicted here. On both register and login, res.data.accessToken (also set as an httpOnly cookie server-side) is written to localStorage.setItem('payflow_access_token', ...). This token is never read back anywhere in the frontend (apiClient relies solely on the httpOnly cookie), meaning it is purely redundant, dead state that remains readable by any JavaScript in the origin for the life of the browser profile.
findings.exploit_scenario: Any XSS on the site (e.g. F-008) can run localStorage.getItem('payflow_access_token') and exfiltrate it, defeating the entire point of the httpOnly cookie design and enabling token replay from the attacker's own machine without needing to ride the victim's session via cookies at all.
findings.recommendation: Remove both localStorage.setItem('payflow_access_token', ...) calls in authApi.ts; rely exclusively on the httpOnly cookie.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the file; the token is provably unused after being stored, confirmed via repo-wide search.

findings.title: lookupRecipient returns another user's email, phone, and live wallet balance from an identifier lookup
findings.description: lookupRecipient(callerUserId, rawIdentifier) resolves a recipient by email or phone and returns { name, identifier, email, phone, walletBalance } to the caller, with no relationship, consent, or beneficiary-list check required. Any authenticated user who knows or guesses another user's email/phone can retrieve their PII and current wallet balance.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker calls the recipient-lookup endpoint with a list of candidate emails/phone numbers (e.g. harvested from a breach corpus or guessed). For each valid PayFlow user, the response discloses their phone number, email, and live wallet balance, enabling targeted social-engineering or financial profiling.
findings.recommendation: Return only the minimum needed to confirm a transfer target (e.g. masked name/initial) and drop balance/phone/email from the lookup response; require an existing beneficiary relationship or a rate-limited, audited lookup flow.
findings.confidence_reason: Independently confirmed by direct source read during this review; matches a previously-documented finding in this repo's own git history (vuln-016) that appears not to have been reverted on this branch.

findings.title: Access token returned in JSON response body in addition to httpOnly cookie
findings.description: registerHandler and loginHandler both call res.status(2xx).json({ user, accessToken }) after already setting the httpOnly cookie. This exposes the token to anything that can observe the response (injected scripts via window.fetch/XMLHttpRequest.prototype.open monkey-patching, browser devtools/history, HTTP debugging proxies), independent of the httpOnly cookie protection.
findings.exploit_scenario: A script running in the page context (via XSS such as F-008, a malicious browser extension, or a compromised third-party dependency loaded on the login page) intercepts the fetch/XHR response for /api/auth/login or /register and reads accessToken directly from the JSON body, bypassing httpOnly protection entirely.
findings.recommendation: Stop returning accessToken in the JSON body for the web login/register flow; return only { user } and rely on the httpOnly cookie. If a future non-cookie client genuinely needs a bearer token, serve it from a distinct endpoint.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the controller; impact is bounded by the 15-minute access-token TTL.

findings.title: TOCTOU race between balance check and debit allows concurrent transfers to overdraw a wallet
findings.description: Inside the prisma.$transaction callback, findUniqueOrThrow issues a plain SELECT with no row lock, the balance check runs against that snapshot, then an explicit 100ms sleep (commented as "fraud/velocity screening") widens the window before the decrement UPDATE executes. Under Postgres's default READ COMMITTED isolation, two concurrent createTransfer calls for the same sender can each pass the balance check before either commits.
findings.exploit_scenario: A wallet with balance 1000 fires two concurrent POST /api/transfers requests, each transferring 1000 to different recipients. Both read balance=1000 within the ~100ms window, both pass the check, both decrement — net effect: 2000 transferred out of a wallet that only held 1000, a double-spend manufacturing 1000 units of currency.
findings.recommendation: Use a single conditional UPDATE (`SET balance = balance - :amount WHERE balance >= :amount`, checking affected row count) or lock the sender's row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE / SERIALIZABLE isolation with retry. Add a DB-level CHECK (balance >= 0) constraint as defense-in-depth.
findings.confidence_reason: Code structure and the explicit artificial delay were directly confirmed; the race mechanism follows from Postgres's documented READ COMMITTED behavior with Prisma interactive transactions, reasoned through but not empirically triggered.

findings.title: App runtime DB role granted CREATEDB, not just the migration/shadow-DB user
findings.description: setup-db.sh creates a single Postgres role `payflow` and grants it CREATEDB for Prisma's shadow-database workflow. This is the same role/credential the running application uses for all normal runtime queries via Prisma Client — there is no separate lower-privileged runtime role. CREATEDB is not needed for day-to-day CRUD operations.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the application's DB access is ever abused (e.g. via F-001's SQL injection, or a leaked DATABASE_URL), the attacker inherits CREATEDB along with normal query rights, enabling disk-fill DoS via new databases or broadening foothold if combined with other Postgres misconfigurations.
findings.recommendation: Use two roles: a migration-only role with CREATEDB (never embedded in the running app's DATABASE_URL) and a separate unprivileged application role for the runtime DATABASE_URL.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the script; real but low real-world impact given this is a local-dev-only setup with no network exposure.

findings.title: CORS reflects any Origin with credentials:true, unconditionally in production
findings.description: app.use(cors({ origin: true, credentials: true })) reflects whatever Origin header the caller sends and allows credentials, for every request, with no isProduction gate (contrast with the helmet CSP line directly above it). env.CORS_ORIGIN is defined and clearly intended for an allowlist but is never passed to cors().
findings.exploit_scenario: The access-token cookie is sameSite=lax and scoped to a configurable cookieDomain with no origin pinning at the CORS layer, so any host under the same registrable site (a compromised/XSS'd sibling subdomain, or a stale subdomain takeover) is treated as same-site by the browser, receives the Lax cookie, and — because CORS reflects its Origin and allows credentials — can read the JSON response cross-origin, exposing wallet/transaction data.
findings.recommendation: Replace origin: true with an explicit allowlist built from env.CORS_ORIGIN, gated behind !isProduction the same way the helmet CSP line is.
findings.confidence_reason: The misconfiguration itself is directly confirmed; the practical exploitability is moderated by the sameSite cookie attributes, which narrow the attack to same-site (not fully cross-site) scenarios, hence a mid-range confidence despite the clear code defect.

findings.title: jsonwebtoken pinned to 8.5.1, the last version before several CVE fixes in 9.0.0
findings.description: jsonwebtoken <=8.5.1 (fixed in 9.0.0) carries documented issues including CVE-2022-23540 (signature-verification bypass when secretOrPublicKey is an object), CVE-2022-23539 (weak validation of the algorithms option), and CVE-2022-23529 (prototype-pollution-driven code execution via a dynamic kid-driven key-resolution callback). The app's actual usage (tokens.ts) signs/verifies with a single static string secret and no dynamic key-resolution callback, so the highest-severity vectors tied to dynamic key lookups have no direct trigger path today; algorithms is also not explicitly restricted in the verify call.
findings.exploit_scenario: Low direct exploitability today given the static-secret usage pattern, but the package is one dependency-graph change away from real exposure: any future code path that resolves the verification key dynamically (JWKS support, multi-tenant keys) would immediately inherit these CVEs on this pinned version.
findings.recommendation: Restore jsonwebtoken to ^9.0.3 or latest 9.x, and explicitly pass algorithms: ['HS256'] to jwt.verify() to remove algorithm-confusion risk regardless of library version.
findings.confidence_reason: Version and named CVEs directly confirmed; confidence moderated because the current call pattern doesn't trigger the most severe of them today.

findings.title: Registration endpoint reveals whether a specific email or phone is already registered
findings.description: register() distinguishes the conflict reason: `existing.email === input.email ? 'Email is already registered' : 'Phone number is already registered'`, exposed via ConflictError with code ALREADY_REGISTERED from the unauthenticated POST /api/auth/register endpoint.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker submits candidate emails (with a filler phone number) to /api/auth/register and reads the response message to confirm whether that email already has a PayFlow account, building a list of confirmed users for phishing (compounding F-009).
findings.recommendation: Return a generic conflict message that doesn't specify which field matched.
findings.confidence_reason: Directly confirmed by reading the exact lines; low severity since it only leaks account existence, not credentials.

findings.title: trust proxy: 1 lets a client-supplied X-Forwarded-For spoof req.ip, potentially bypassing IP-keyed rate limiting
findings.description: app.set('trust proxy', 1) tells Express to trust exactly one hop of X-Forwarded-For when computing req.ip. Both apiLimiter and the unused authLimiter key on req.ip by default. No Dockerfile/reverse-proxy config exists in this repo, so the actual deployment topology (how many real proxy hops exist, if any) is unverified — if it doesn't match exactly one trusted hop, an attacker can set an arbitrary X-Forwarded-For header per request to bucket each under a distinct rate-limit key.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker sends repeated POST /api/auth/login requests, each with a different fabricated X-Forwarded-For header. If the network path doesn't strip/overwrite this header, every request is treated as coming from a different IP, defeating IP-based rate limiting and enabling unthrottled brute force.
findings.recommendation: Verify the exact proxy chain in each deployment environment and set trust proxy to match precisely, or key rate limiting on a value not attacker-controllable post-auth.
findings.confidence_reason: The code-level condition is confirmed, but actual exploitability depends on the (currently undocumented/nonexistent) deployment topology, which lowers confidence.

findings.title: No idempotency protection on transfer or top-up allows a client retry to duplicate a money movement
findings.description: Neither createTransfer nor addMoney accepts or checks any idempotency key. Each call unconditionally creates a new Transaction row and mutates the wallet balance. A duplicate HTTP request for the same logical operation (client retry-on-timeout, double-tap, proxy replay) is processed as an entirely independent, fully-effective transfer or top-up.
findings.exploit_scenario: A user taps "Send" on a slow network; the request is accepted but the response is delayed/lost, so the client retries. Both requests independently execute a full debit/credit, charging the user twice for a single intended transfer.
findings.recommendation: Accept a client-generated idempotency key on both endpoints, persist it within the same DB transaction as the balance mutation, and short-circuit with the original result when the same key is replayed.
findings.confidence_reason: The design gap is confirmed, but this is more of a reliability/fraud-adjacent concern than a directly attacker-triggered exploit, hence moderate-low confidence.

findings.title: Sender/receiver wallet ACTIVE status is checked before the transaction but not re-verified at the point of debit/credit
findings.description: The sender's and receiver's wallet status are each checked once before the DB transaction begins. Inside the actual prisma.$transaction block, the sender wallet is re-fetched but only its balance is checked — status is never re-verified for either party immediately before the writes.
findings.exploit_scenario: A fraud-review process suspends a wallet in the narrow window between the pre-transaction status check and the transaction's write. The transfer can still complete on a wallet that is, at the moment of the write, supposed to be frozen.
findings.recommendation: Re-check status === 'ACTIVE' for both wallets using the freshly-read rows inside the transaction callback, immediately before applying balance updates.
findings.confidence_reason: Narrow race window requiring precise timing with an external suspension event; plausible but speculative.

findings.title: verifyOrigin fails open when the Origin header is absent
findings.description: The check only rejects when an Origin header is present and mismatched; if no Origin header is sent at all, the request passes through unchecked. Modern browsers reliably attach Origin on cross-site mutating requests, so this is not obviously reachable from a standard browser CSRF vector, and the middleware is currently unused anyway (F-010).
findings.exploit_scenario: If F-010 is fixed by wiring this middleware in as-is, any mutating request that reaches the server without an Origin header (rare in modern browsers, but possible via some non-browser/legacy-client paths) would skip the check entirely.
findings.recommendation: When wiring this middleware in, reject-by-default: require Origin (or fall back to Referer) to be present and match, rather than only rejecting on a present-but-mismatched value.
findings.confidence_reason: Latent since the middleware isn't active; low practical reachability from standard browsers even if activated as-is.

findings.title: Email fields have no max-length bound
findings.description: z.email() is used in registerSchema, loginSchema, and the shared identifierSchema without a .max(...) bound, unlike name and phone in the same schemas. The global express.json({ limit: '32kb' }) body cap prevents truly massive payloads, but a multi-KB email value can still reach an unbounded `email String @unique` column.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker registers with an email value padded to thousands of characters before the @, which passes z.email() and is stored/indexed as a unique column, potentially causing oversized index entries or inconsistent downstream behavior.
findings.recommendation: Add a .max(254) bound (RFC 5321 practical limit) to email fields.
findings.confidence_reason: Real but low-impact gap; bounded further by the global body-size limit.

findings.title: Password hash comparison uses non-constant-time ===
findings.description: verifyPassword compares candidate === hash using native string equality, which short-circuits on the first differing character — a timing side channel layered on top of the already-weak SHA-256 scheme (F-002).
findings.exploit_scenario: A remote attacker with very precise timing measurement could in theory attempt to recover hash bytes incrementally, though this is extremely hard to exploit over a real network due to jitter and the fixed-length hex digest limiting usable signal.
findings.recommendation: Use crypto.timingSafeEqual on fixed-length buffers, in addition to fixing the underlying hash algorithm per F-002.
findings.confidence_reason: Real defense-in-depth gap but not demonstrated as a practical remote attack.

findings.title: Pino redaction list omits token/secret field names
findings.description: The redact.paths list covers password/currentPassword/newPassword/passwordHash and cookie/authorization headers, but not accessToken, refreshToken, token, rawToken, tokenHash, or secret. No current code path logs a full request body or token-bearing object, so this is latent rather than actively exploitable today.
findings.exploit_scenario: A future code change adds logger.debug({ body: req.body }) to a login/refresh handler for troubleshooting. Because token fields aren't redaction targets, raw bearer/session tokens would be written to log files in plaintext.
findings.recommendation: Extend the redact paths to include *.accessToken, *.refreshToken, *.token, *.rawToken, *.tokenHash, *.secret, as defense-in-depth against future logging additions.
findings.confidence_reason: No current trigger path exists; purely a latent hardening gap.

findings.title: LOGIN_FAILURE audit entries store attacker-supplied email with no read/export endpoint
findings.description: On a failed login with a non-existent account, writeAuditLog stores the raw, unauthenticated, user-submitted email in AuditLog.metadata. No findMany/export route reads the AuditLog table anywhere in the codebase, so this is a latent-exposure issue only.
findings.exploit_scenario: No direct exploit today since there is no read/export endpoint. Risk would materialize only if an admin audit-log viewer is added later without re-reviewing what's stored.
findings.recommendation: No immediate action required. If an audit-log read/export endpoint is ever added, ensure it's admin-only and consider masking raw attempted-email values.
findings.confidence_reason: Confirmed latent-only via repo-wide search for AuditLog reads; no live exposure path exists.
